Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Optical coherence tomography showed good foveal contour, no macular edema or epiretinal membrane, and final best-corrected visual acuity of 20/300 OD and 20/20 OS.

A 13-year-old male presented with a 7-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging mass in the right parotid region. He underwent surgery at a local hospital 6 months prior. The pathological diagnosis was lymphadenitis. However, the mass persistently enlarged after the surgery. When the patient visited our hospital, a bulging mass (approximately 5 × 4 cm) was palpable in the right parotid region, which was firm, nontender, and immobile. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial computed tomography showed an ill-defined 3.6 × 3.2 × 2.7-cm soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland, with indistinct borders at the posterior margin of the right masseter muscle. Multiple mildly enlarged lymph nodes were noted at the inferior pole of the parotid gland and adjacent to the superior margin of the lesion (Figure 1A). The patient underwent right parotid mass resection and total parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection. Intraoperative findings indicated a firm mass located within the superficial parotid lobe. It had adhered to the surface of the mandibular ramus, with indistinct planes of dissection from the masseter and temporalis muscles. Histopathology results demonstrated that a circumscribed mass was surrounded by a thick fibrous pseudocapsule, and the tumor was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces and a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff were noted. The tumor showed focal sclerosing changes and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells appeared as mild atypia, while mitoses were rarely identified (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1 positivity.

Your point about ALK positivity and recurrence risk is valid, but the histopathology shows a circumscribed mass with a thick fibrous pseudocapsule, and we achieved a total parotidectomy with clear margins. The lymph nodes were mildly enlarged, which is consistent with the inflammatory nature of IMT, and there's no evidence of necrosis or high mitotic activity. Therefore, I still believe surveillance is adequate, given the complete resection and low-grade features.

[AI assistant's reply]
I agree that the circumscribed appearance and low-grade histology are reassuring. However, the preoperative CT described an ill-defined mass with indistinct borders and adherence to muscle, which can sometimes indicate a more locally aggressive phenotype despite the pseudocapsule. Given the prior recurrence after initial surgery, would you at least recommend a shorter interval for the first few follow-up scans to ensure early detection of any local regrowth?

He remained free of recurrence on regular clinical and computed tomography (CT) surveillance but continued daily heavy alcohol consumption. Three years later, he developed progressive frailty with 3 months of reduced oral intake. Neurologic examination revealed diminished superficial sensation, dysesthesia, and impaired proprioception in the lower extremities, consistent with sensory ataxia in a polyneuropathy pattern. A 74-year-old man was referred for evaluation of suspected interstitial keratitis of the right eye. He noted progressive blurry vision but denied eye pain or antecedent trauma. Visual acuity on presentation was 20/50 OD and 20/20 OS. Medical history was remarkable for a 10–pack-year smoking history, stable thoracic aortic aneurysm, and hypertension. There was no history of contact lens wear. A review of systems was negative for a history of eye infections, travel outside of the US, or hearing changes. Limited workup was positive for herpes simplex virus 1 (HSV1) and HSV2 immunoglobulin G (IgG) and negative for antinuclear antibody (ANA), antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA), rapid plasma reagin (RPR), anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide (CCP), and interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis. Good point about the limitations of RPR and IGRA. Given that, and the lesion's persistence, I'll proceed with the biopsy. It will provide histopathology and allow for direct staining and culture for atypical organisms, including acid-fast bacilli or spirochetes.

That's a sound plan. The biopsy will be crucial for ruling out atypical infections like atypical mycobacteria, Nocardia, or even a non-infectious inflammatory process such as a localized corneal dystrophy or deposit. Please ensure samples are sent for standard bacterial, fungal, and mycobacterial cultures, as well as histopathology with special stains.

Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. Observe unless retained PFO incites intraocular inflammation or vitreoretinal interface abnormalities PFV is a congenital ocular anomaly occurring in 0.064% to 5% of births, characterized by the failure of regression of the embryonic hyaloid vasculature, resulting in vascular membranes between the lens and optic nerve.1PFV is classified into 3 categories based on the location of abnormalities: anterior (25%), posterior (12%), and combined (60%). Given the presence of anterior segment abnormalities, secondary intraocular lens implantation (choice C) is not considered the optimal management strategy.1,2PFV is also associated with systemic conditions, such as trisomy 13, trisomy 15, Aicardi syndrome, Norrie disease, Walker-Warburg syndrome, and osteoporosis-pseudoglioma syndrome.2 Historically, surgery was not recommended for PFV; however, advances in surgical techniques and instrumentation have significantly improved outcomes. The primary reason for surgical intervention is to reduce the risk of deprivation amblyopia, particularly when diagnosed early. Surgical management is challenging due to a high risk of peripheral and anterior retinal tears, often necessitating PFO for retinal stabilization. Therefore, returning to the operating room immediately for PFO removal (choice A) is not considered optimal. Additionally, there is currently no evidence that topical corticosteroids (choice D) facilitate PFO absorption.2-5 PFO is associated with potential intraocular complications. Acute postoperative toxicity, including retinal damage and optic nerve atrophy, may occur due to chemical impurities or residual acid or alcohol contaminants, even when PFO is removed during surgery. Long-term retention may result in macrophage infiltration at the PFO vitreous interface, triggering inflammation. Prolonged intraocular PFO has also been linked to epiretinal membrane formation, retinal atrophy, and increased risk of retinal redetachment.6,7 Conversely, some studies report no clinical, electrophysiological, or histological evidence of toxicity after 48 hours of PFO presence in rabbit models. Isolated cases have demonstrated prolonged tolerance: one case reported retained PFO for 9 years postoperatively without cytotoxic effects. A multicenter study of 555 patients undergoing surgery found a 7.4% incidence of retained PFO. After 10 years, retained PFO was not associated with higher rates of redetachment or poor visual outcomes.8-10 Based on current evidence, observation (choice B) may be a reasonable strategy in pediatric patients with retained PFO following complex retinal surgery, provided there is no associated inflammation or intraocular pressure elevation. The patient was followed up with every 6 months for 14 years to monitor for PFO toxicity. Visual acuity steadily improved with amblyopia therapy—including glasses, patching, and contact lens use for secondary aphakia—and eventually stabilized with no signs of anterior or posterior chamber inflammation. Fundus photographs revealed PFO bubbles in the inferior retina (Figure 2). Optical coherence tomography showed good foveal contour, no macular edema or epiretinal membrane, and final best-corrected visual acuity of 20/300 OD and 20/20 OS.
